story.headline: US retail sales rose a little more than forecast in October, so bets on a December Fed hike held and the dollar rose a seventh day. The euro and Aussie fell to their lowest in months.

reads.policy: Firm US retail sales kept a December Fed hike near certain, and nothing overnight changed the picture elsewhere. Europe, Britain and Japan are still expected to hike, Canada and New Zealand look more likely to wait, and Australia's board is split. US rates still look set to rise fastest, which keeps favouring the dollar.
reads.growth: US shoppers kept spending in October, with spending outside cars stronger than expected, so the US economy still looks firmer than most. Japan's economy shrank in the summer, euro-area factories are barely growing and China's demand is soft. That gap supports the dollar against the euro, yen and Aussie.
reads.inflation: UK pay growth cooled in line with forecasts, so UK inflation figures on Wednesday will matter more for the pound. New Zealand businesses' inflation expectations barely moved, giving its central bank no new reason to hike. US inflation is still well above the Fed's goal, which keeps up the pressure to raise rates.
reads.risk: Monday's sharp fall in US tech shares spread to Asia overnight and briefly lifted the yen. New Iranian drone attacks on Bahrain and tanker strikes in the Gulf added to the unease without sparking wider fear. The Aussie and kiwi, which track market mood, slipped to their lowest in months.
reads.tot: Oil fell further overnight on the supply-surplus outlook, then bounced as attacks on tankers kept coming. That keeps some support under the Canadian dollar. Gold stays near a 13-month low, which adds to the Aussie's troubles.
reads.positioning: The latest weekly figures show hedge funds leaning toward the dollar and the pound and against the euro, the kiwi and the Canadian dollar, with bets against the kiwi growing fastest. Big long-term investors take the other side on the euro, pound and Aussie. Where the two groups disagree, a surprise could set off a fast unwind.
reads.fiscal: Record US government borrowing keeps long-term US borrowing costs above 5%, and firm retail sales nudged them a little higher. Higher yields support the dollar for now, but a growing deficit is a worry if buyers start asking for more. France's debt troubles keep weighing on the euro.

fed.summary: The Federal Reserve held rates on October 28 with two officials voting to hike. Hot inflation and firm consumer spending have made a December hike all but certain and lifted the dollar to its highest since April 2025.
fed.priced: December: hike all but certain, with a half-point move a small minority bet. More hikes expected next year.
fed.why: US inflation is running at about twice the Fed's 2% goal. October retail sales showed shoppers still spending, so nothing argues for waiting.
fed.watch: Minutes of the October meeting Wednesday at 1:00 PM CT and weekly jobless claims Thursday at 7:30 AM CT. The decision is December 9.

boc.summary: The Bank of Canada raised rates to 2.50% in October and said more may be needed. October inflation held at 3.1% with core prices near 2%, so a December hike now looks less likely than not.
boc.priced: December: hold more likely, with a hike a bit under even odds.
boc.why: Energy is lifting headline inflation, but core prices are calm and the economy is shedding jobs, so the bank can afford to wait.
boc.watch: Canada's November jobs figures on December 4 and the path of oil prices. The decision is December 9.

rbnz.summary: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand held at 2.75% in October in a narrow vote. Rising unemployment has made a December hike less certain, and the kiwi sits near its lowest in more than a year and a half.
rbnz.priced: December: hike possible but not fully expected.
rbnz.why: Inflation pressures argue for a hike, but unemployment at its highest since 2015 argues for waiting. Businesses' inflation expectations barely moved in the latest survey.
rbnz.watch: Governor Anna Breman speaks Wednesday at 12:00 PM CT. The decision is December 9.

ecb.summary: The European Central Bank held at 2.50% in October and a December hike is widely expected. Economists see it as the last for now, which leaves the euro trailing as US rates keep rising, and it has fallen below $1.10.
ecb.priced: December: hike widely expected, possibly the last for a while.
ecb.why: Euro-area inflation is about double the bank's goal, but factories are barely growing and France's debt worries linger, so the bank has little room to keep hiking.
ecb.watch: The bank's Financial Stability Review Wednesday at 3:00 AM CT, then President Christine Lagarde speaks at 8:25 AM CT. The decision is December 17.

boj.summary: The Bank of Japan holds at 1.25%, far below other major banks, and is expected to hike in December. Board member Hajime Takata called for an early move even though Japan's economy shrank slightly in the summer.
boj.why: The weak yen is pushing import costs and prices up, and Takata says hikes are needed so it does not weaken further. A shrinking economy is the main reason to wait.
boj.watch: Whether Japan buys yen if the dollar tops 160 again, and Governor Kazuo Ueda's speech on November 30. The decision is December 18.

rba.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised rates to 4.85% on November 3, the highest among the major banks, in a six-to-three vote. Big Australian banks think that is the peak, and the Aussie has fallen to its lowest since January.
rba.priced: December: a hold expected, with rates seen at their peak.
rba.why: Most board members worry inflation is too high, but three feared a sharper slowdown, and unemployment is at a five-year high.
rba.watch: Australian wages Tuesday at 6:30 PM CT and October jobs figures Wednesday at 6:30 PM CT. The decision is December 8.

boe.summary: The Bank of England raised Bank Rate to 4.00% on November 5 and said more may follow. Markets still expect a second hike in December, and UK pay growth cooled only as much as forecast.
boe.priced: December: a second hike more likely than not.
boe.why: High energy costs from the Middle East conflict keep UK inflation up, and pay is cooling only slowly.
boe.watch: UK inflation for October Wednesday at 1:00 AM CT, then Governor Andrew Bailey speaks at 1:30 AM and 9:00 AM CT. The decision is December 17.

snb.summary: The Swiss National Bank holds its rate at zero and can sell francs if they get too strong. Low Swiss inflation means no hike is in sight.
snb.why: Swiss inflation is low, so the bank has no reason to raise rates and some room to cut if the franc climbs.
snb.watch: Any flare-up that sends money into the franc. The decision is December 10.

USD.summary: The dollar sits third on the board. High US interest rates support it, while large budget deficits weigh a little. Firm October retail sales kept a December Fed hike near certain.

EUR.summary: The euro sits just below the middle of the board. Cheaper oil helps the euro area, but budget worries in France and rates below most of the others hold it back. Rising US rates pushed it below $1.10 for the first time since April 2025.

GBP.summary: The pound sits at the top of the board, just ahead of the Aussie, because UK interest rates are among the highest of the eight after the Bank of England's hike to 4.00%. UK inflation figures on Wednesday will help decide whether a second hike comes in December.

JPY.summary: The yen sits second from the bottom because Japanese interest rates are far below the others and inflation is close to the Bank of Japan's goal. A likely December rate hike and warnings from Japan's finance minister only just keep the dollar below 160 yen.

CHF.summary: The franc sits at the bottom of the board. Swiss interest rates are the lowest of the eight and inflation is too low to need higher rates. The dollar has climbed to its highest against it in about 18 months.

AUD.summary: The Aussie sits second on the board thanks to the highest interest rates among the major central banks. It still fell to its lowest since January as US rates rose, Chinese demand softened and gold slid.

CAD.summary: The Canadian dollar sits near the bottom of the board. Falling oil prices hurt Canada's exports, and recent Canadian data has mostly missed forecasts. The US dollar is just above its October high against it.

NZD.summary: The kiwi sits in the middle of the board. Firm prices for New Zealand's dairy exports help, and its rates are close to the middle of the eight. Rising US rates have kept it near its lowest in more than a year and a half.
